title: From information to sample size
text:
A group sequential design is solved on the \(Z\) scale (Information). Its output is the drift \(\eta = \theta_1\sqrt{I_{\max}}\) that gives the required power, so the maximum information is
\[
I_{\max} = \left(\frac{\eta}{\theta_1}\right)^2 = R \cdot I_{\text{fix}},
\]
where \(R\) is the inflation factor. The endpoint only enters when \(I\) is translated into observations. At look \(k\) the study needs \(t_k\) times the maximum.

title: From information to sample size
text:
Time-to-event endpoints
For survival outcomes, information is carried by events, not patients. With allocation \(r:1\) and a log-rank test, Schoenfeld (1983) gives
\[
D = I_{\max}\,\frac{(1+r)^2}{r} = \frac{\eta^2 (1+r)^2}{r\,(\ln \mathrm{HR})^2}
\]
events. Freedman (1982) proposed the alternative \(D = \eta^2 (1 + r\,\mathrm{HR})^2 / \{r(1-\mathrm{HR})^2\}\). The analyses are scheduled after \(t_k D\) events.
How many patients give \(D\) events, and when each look happens, depend on accrual, follow-up and dropout. With exponential survival (hazard \(\lambda\)), exponential dropout (hazard \(\gamma\)), uniform accrual over a period \(A\) and a minimum follow-up \(F\), the probability that a patient’s event is observed by the end of the study is
\[
P(\text{event}) = \frac{\lambda}{\lambda+\gamma}\left[1 - \frac{e^{-(\lambda+\gamma)F} - e^{-(\lambda+\gamma)(A+F)}}{(\lambda+\gamma)A}\right],
\]
averaged over the arms according to the allocation. Then \(N = D / P(\text{event})\) (Lachin and Foulkes 1986; Lakatos 1988). The expected number of events by calendar time \(\tau\) follows from the same integral truncated at \(\tau\). Solving \(E[D(\tau_k)] = t_k D\) gives the expected calendar time of each look (Kim and Tsiatis 1990). The same model can instead be solved for the accrual duration (given a rate) or for the follow-up (given \(N\)).

title: Futility boundaries
text: Efficacy boundaries alone never shorten a trial of an ineffective treatment: under \(H_0\) it runs to its maximum size. A futility boundary \(a_k\) stops the study when the evidence of benefit is weak — for a one-sided design, when \(Z_k \le a_k\). Patients are no longer randomised to a treatment that does not work, and resources are freed (Lachin 2005). The price is a small loss of power, which is recovered by a slightly larger maximum sample size.

title: Futility boundaries
text:
Binding or non-binding?

Binding futility: the efficacy boundaries are computed assuming the trial stops whenever the futility boundary is crossed. The efficacy boundaries are slightly lower. But if the monitoring committee decides to continue after crossing the futility boundary, the type I error is no longer controlled.
Non-binding futility: the efficacy boundaries are computed ignoring the futility rule, so \(\alpha\) is controlled whether or not the rule is followed. The actual type I error is slightly below \(\alpha\) when the rule is followed. This is the usual choice in confirmatory trials, because a committee must remain free to weigh other evidence (U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2019).

Power is always computed assuming the futility rule is followed.

title: Futility boundaries
section: Ways to define the futility boundary
text:
Ways to define the futility boundary
Beta spending. The type II error is spent like \(\alpha\), with any of the spending families. At look \(k\), \(a_k\) solves
\[
P_{\theta_1}\!\left(\text{continue to look } k,\ Z_k \le a_k\right) = \beta(t_k) - \beta(t_{k-1}).
\]
The maximum information is then chosen so that the two boundaries meet at the final look, \(a_K = b_K\). That gives power exactly \(1-\beta\) (Pampallona et al. 2001).
Fixed z-values. For example, stop if \(Z < 0\) (the estimate points the wrong way) at the halfway look. The maximum information is solved for power.
Conditional power. Stop if the probability of eventually rejecting \(H_0\), given the current data, falls below a threshold \(\gamma\) (Gordon Lan et al. 1982; Lachin 2005). Under the current trend and with only the final analysis remaining, this converts to the \(z\)-bound
\[
a_k = \sqrt{t_k}\,\left(b_K - \sqrt{1 - t_k}\; z_{1-\gamma}\right).
\]
Pampallona–Tsiatis. A power-family shape for both boundaries, solved jointly so that they meet at the last look (Pampallona and Tsiatis 1994).

text:
When a trial stops because its \(Z\) statistic crossed a boundary, it has been selected for being extreme. The ordinary estimate at the stopping look is therefore biased away from zero. title: Inference after a sequential test
text:
Repeated confidence intervals
Jennison and Turnbull (1989) proposed repeated confidence intervals (RCIs): a sequence of intervals that contains \(\theta\) simultaneously at every look with probability \(1-\alpha\),
\[
\hat\theta_k \pm \frac{c_k}{\sqrt{I_k}},
\]
where \(c_k\) are the boundaries of a two-sided level-\(\alpha\) group sequential test. Because the coverage is simultaneous, an RCI is valid whatever the stopping decision — even if the monitoring committee departs from the boundaries. That makes RCIs the natural interval to report at interim looks. At the final analysis they are conservative.

title: Inference after a sequential test
section: Exact inference at the end of the trial
text:
Exact inference at the end of the trial
For the final report, the sample space of outcomes \((k^*, z^*)\) — stopping look and statistic — must be ordered to define what “more extreme” means. The stagewise ordering ranks outcomes first by how early the efficacy boundary was crossed, then by \(z\) within the same look (Fairbanks and Madsen 1982; Tsiatis et al. 1984):

p-value. \(P_{H_0}\) of stopping for efficacy earlier than \(k^*\), or at \(k^*\) with a statistic at least \(z^*\).
Confidence interval. All \(\theta\) for which the same probability, computed under \(\theta\), lies between \(\alpha/2\) and \(1-\alpha/2\).
Median-unbiased estimate. The \(\theta\) at which that probability is exactly 0.5.

The stagewise ordering depends only on the looks already done: it does not need the future schedule. Its p-value agrees with the test decision. Other orderings (likelihood ratio, maximum likelihood estimate) and bias-adjusted estimators exist, each with its own properties (Emerson and Fleming 1990; Robertson et al. 2023a, 2023b). All of these quantities are computed with the same numerical engine as the boundaries, by solving over \(\theta\).

title: Inference after a sequential test
text:
Reporting
The CONSORT extension for adaptive designs asks for the planned and actual looks, the boundaries, the reason for stopping, and estimates and intervals that account for the design (Dimairo et al. 2020).

title: Glossary
text:
Alpha spending function

The cumulative type I error \(\alpha(t)\) allowed to be spent by information fraction \(t\) (Alpha spending).

Always-valid p-value

A p-value that remains valid whatever the stopping time; the reciprocal of the running maximum of an e-process (Anytime-valid).

B-value

\(B(t) = Z(t)\sqrt t\); a Brownian motion with drift \(\eta\) under the canonical distribution (Information).

Beta spending

Spending of the type II error over the looks, used to build futility boundaries (Futility).

Binding / non-binding futility

Whether the efficacy boundaries assume the futility rule is always obeyed (binding) or ignore it (non-binding) (Futility).

Boundary

The critical value of the test statistic at a look. Crossing the efficacy boundary rejects \(H_0\); crossing the futility boundary stops for lack of effect.

Canonical joint distribution

\(Z_k \sim N(\theta\sqrt{I_k}, 1)\) with \(\operatorname{Cov}(Z_j, Z_k) = \sqrt{I_j/I_k}\); the common structure of almost all sequential statistics (Information).

Christmas-tree correction

Adjustment of continuous boundaries (such as the triangular test’s) for discrete looks (Triangular tests).

Conditional power

Probability of rejecting \(H_0\) at the end, given the current data and an assumed effect (Monitoring).

Confidence sequence

Intervals that contain the parameter at all sample sizes simultaneously with probability \(1-\alpha\) (Anytime-valid).

Data monitoring committee (DMC)

Independent committee that reviews unblinded interim results and recommends continuation or stopping.

Drift

\(\eta = \theta\sqrt{I_{\max}}\), the expected value of the B-value at the end of the study.

E-value, e-process

A non-negative statistic with null expectation at most 1; a sequence of them forming a supermartingale (Anytime-valid).

Expected sample size (ASN)

Average sample size of a sequential design under a given true effect; also called average sample number.

Inflation factor

Ratio of the maximum information of a sequential design to that of the fixed-sample design with the same \(\alpha\) and power.

Information, information fraction

\(I = 1/\operatorname{Var}(\hat\theta)\); \(t_k = I_k/I_{\max}\) (Information).

Inner wedge

Futility region \(|Z_k| < a_k\) of a two-sided design (Futility).

Look (interim analysis)

One of the \(K\) analyses of the accumulating data.

MaxSPRT

Maximised sequential probability ratio test for safety surveillance (MaxSPRT).

Median-unbiased estimate

Estimate whose sampling distribution has median \(\theta\), computed under the stagewise ordering (Inference).

Predictive power (predictive probability)

Conditional power averaged over the posterior distribution of the effect (Monitoring, Bayesian).

Repeated confidence interval

Sequence of intervals with simultaneous coverage across looks (Inference).

SPRT

Wald’s sequential probability ratio test (SPRT).

Stagewise ordering

Ordering of outcomes by stopping look, then by \(Z\), used for exact p-values and confidence intervals after a sequential test (Inference).

Stochastic curtailment

Stopping when conditional power makes the final decision nearly certain.

Triangular test

Whitehead’s closed sequential test with straight-line boundaries on the \((V, Z)\) plane (Triangular tests).

title: Why sequential analysis?
text:
A randomised trial recruits patients over several years. Its data monitoring committee (DMC) meets every few months. Patients are entitled to stop receiving an inferior treatment as soon as the evidence is clear, and funders do not want to pay for recruitment that can no longer change the conclusion (DeMets and Ellenberg 2016; Whitehead 2004). The same pressure exists in cohort studies, vaccine safety surveillance and laboratory experiments.
The difficulty is statistical. Each look is a new chance of a false-positive result. If the analyst tests the accumulating data at the usual 5 % level every time and stops at the first significant result, the overall probability of a false positive is no longer 5 %.

title: Why sequential analysis?
text:
What a sequential design specifies
A sequential design fixes, before any data are seen:

When to look. The number of analyses \(K\) and their timing, expressed as the information fraction \(t_k\) — the proportion of the final statistical information available at look \(k\) (see Information).
When to stop. Boundaries for the test statistic. Crossing the efficacy boundary stops the study and rejects \(H_0\). Crossing an optional futility boundary stops it for lack of effect.
How large the study may become. The maximum sample size (or number of events), chosen so that the power is still \(1-\beta\) despite the stricter boundaries.

The boundaries are calculated so that the probability of ever crossing the efficacy boundary is exactly \(\alpha\) when \(H_0\) is true.

title: Why sequential analysis?
text:
Benefits and costs
Benefits. The expected sample size is smaller than that of a fixed-sample study with the same power, often by 20–40 % when the treatment works (Jennison and Turnbull 2000; Todd et al. 2001). Participants are exposed to an inferior treatment for less time, and answers arrive earlier.
Costs.

The maximum sample size is larger than the fixed one; the ratio is the inflation factor.
The design needs a monitoring structure (a DMC, data cleaning at each look) and pre-specified rules (International Council for Harmonisation 1998; U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2019).
A study stopped early for benefit tends to overestimate the effect. The naive estimate at the stopping look is biased, markedly so when few events have accrued (Bassler et al. 2010). Correct inference after a sequential test needs special methods (Inference).

title: Why sequential analysis?
text:
Where to go next
The next page, Information, explains the statistical structure — the canonical joint distribution — that makes all these calculations possible for any endpoint. For book-length treatments, see Jennison and Turnbull (2000), Whitehead (1997),  (2006) and Wassmer and Brannath (2016). Short reviews are Todd (2007) and Lakens (2014).

title: Sequential Methods: an Introduction
text:
Clinical trials and epidemiological studies collect their data over months or years. It is natural — and often an ethical obligation — to look at the results before the end. Looking repeatedly, however, changes the error rates of the analysis. Sequential methods plan those looks in advance so that the overall probability of a false positive stays at its nominal level, and so that the study still has the power it was designed for.
This tutorial introduces the main families of sequential methods. It is written for applied researchers — clinicians, epidemiologists, psychologists, students — who know the basics of hypothesis testing and want to design or monitor a sequential study. It accompanies jmsequential, a jamovi module that implements the methods described here.

title: Anytime-valid inference
Anytime-valid inference
Anytime-valid inference
text:
E-values and e-processes
An e-value is a non-negative statistic \(E\) whose expectation under \(H_0\) is at most 1. By Markov’s inequality, \(P_{H_0}(E \ge 1/\alpha) \le \alpha\). A sequence of e-values that forms a non-negative supermartingale under \(H_0\) — an e-process — satisfies Ville’s inequality:
\[
P_{H_0}\!\left(\exists\, n:\ E_n \ge 1/\alpha\right) \le \alpha .
\]
The data can be monitored after every observation and the test rejects the first time \(E_n \ge 1/\alpha\) (20 for \(\alpha = 0.05\)). The type I error stays controlled even if the study continues beyond any planned size. E-values can also be multiplied across independent studies (Vovk and Wang 2021; Grünwald et al. 2024).
Any likelihood ratio against a fixed alternative is an e-process — Wald’s SPRT statistic is one. Averaging the likelihood ratio over a distribution of alternatives keeps the property. For normal data with variance \(\sigma^2\) and a normal mixing distribution with variance \(\tau^2\), this gives Robbins’ mixture likelihood ratio (Robbins 1970):
\[
E_n = \sqrt{\frac{\sigma^2}{\sigma^2 + n\tau^2}}\;
\exp\!\left(\frac{n^2\tau^2(\bar x_n - \theta_0)^2}{2\sigma^2(\sigma^2 + n\tau^2)}\right).
\]
Its reciprocal gives the always-valid p-value used by several industry A/B-testing platforms (the mixture SPRT, mSPRT) (Johari et al. 2022).

title: Anytime-valid inference
text:
Confidence sequences
Inverting an e-process gives a confidence sequence: a sequence of intervals that contains \(\theta\) at all sample sizes simultaneously with probability \(1-\alpha\). For the normal mixture above, the interval at sample size \(n\) is
\[
\bar x_n \pm \sqrt{\frac{2\sigma^2(\sigma^2 + n\tau^2)}{n^2\tau^2}\,
\ln\!\left(\frac{\sqrt{1 + n\tau^2/\sigma^2}}{\alpha}\right)} .
\]
Nonparametric and asymptotic versions exist (Howard et al. 2021; Waudby-Smith et al. 2024).
The price of this flexibility is width. A fixed-sample confidence interval is valid only at the one sample size chosen in advance; a confidence sequence is valid at all of them.





















Figure 1: Half-width of a 95 % confidence sequence (normal mixture tuned for n = 100) and of the fixed-sample 95 % confidence interval, sigma = 1.



At the tuning point \(n = 100\) the confidence sequence is 55 % wider than the fixed interval.

title: Anytime-valid inference
text:
Safe tests
Grünwald et al. (2024) construct safe tests: e-values that grow as fast as possible under the alternative (GROW optimality), for the \(t\)-test, 2×2 tables and other standard settings. An anytime-valid log-rank test exists for survival data (Schure et al. 2024). ALL-IN meta-analysis applies the same ideas to living systematic reviews (Schure and Grünwald 2022).
Compared with a well-planned group sequential design, anytime-valid methods need a somewhat larger sample at a given horizon. In exchange, the analysis plan does not have to be fixed in advance.

The Anytime-Valid Monitoring analysis computes its operating characteristics exactly: with a known SD, “reject when \(E_n \ge 20\)” is a boundary on \(|z_n|\), handled by the same numerical integration as group sequential designs.

Testing after every observation needs 54 patients to reach 80 % power, against 32 for the fixed design. Under the design effect the test usually stops much earlier: the expected sample size is 36.6 and the median 32. The R package safestats estimates the same design by simulation (55 ± 3 patients). For an unknown SD the analysis simulates the safe \(t\)-test. Two samples with \(d = 0.5\) need 218 patients in total for 80 % power with continuous monitoring, against 130 for the fixed-sample \(t\)-test.

From then on the 95 % confidence sequence excludes 0. The sequential t-test on the same data stops after 41 patients. It is one-sided, bets on the single alternative \(d = 0.5\), and rejects at a likelihood ratio of \((1-\beta)/\alpha = 16\). The mixture e-value is two-sided and spreads its bet over all effect sizes. That costs speed when the true effect is close to the planned one, and gains robustness when it is not.

title: Safety surveillance: the MaxSPRT
text: After a vaccine or drug is licensed, rare adverse events are monitored in near real time in large health-care databases. Each week brings new exposed persons and new events. The question is whether the observed count of an adverse event exceeds what would be expected, and the analysis is repeated every week for months or years (Yih et al. 2011; Nelson et al. 2015). Repeated testing must control the overall false-alarm probability. Unlike a trial, there is no specific alternative: any increase in risk matters.

The question is whether the observed count of an adverse event exceeds what would be expected, and the analysis is repeated every week for months or years (Yih et al. 2011; Nelson et al. 2015). title: Safety surveillance: the MaxSPRT
text:
The maximized SPRT
Kulldorff et al. (2011) replaced the simple alternative of Wald’s SPRT with a composite one, relative risk \(\mathrm{RR} > 1\), and maximised the likelihood ratio over it. For Poisson data, with \(c_t\) observed and \(\mu_t\) expected events by time \(t\),
\[
\mathrm{LLR}_t = \begin{cases} (\mu_t - c_t) + c_t \ln(c_t/\mu_t) & \text{if } c_t > \mu_t,\\
0 & \text{otherwise.} \end{cases}
\]
A signal is raised the first time \(\mathrm{LLR}_t\) reaches a critical value \(\mathrm{CV}\). The critical value is computed exactly so that the probability of any signal before the end of surveillance is \(\alpha\) under \(H_0\). The end of surveillance is defined by an upper limit \(T\) on the expected count. Variants include:

Binomial MaxSPRT for self-controlled and matched designs. Each event falls in the risk window or in a control window, and the matching ratio fixes the null probability.
Conditional MaxSPRT for when the expected counts are estimated from historical data.
Minimum events. A minimum number of events can be required before a signal, which avoids signals from one or two early events.

Continuous versus group monitoring. Testing at every new event maximises timeliness. Testing at fixed intervals (group sequential MaxSPRT) loses little and matches how data arrive in practice (Silva and Kulldorff 2015). The type I error can also be distributed over the looks with an optimal alpha spending (Silva et al. 2020). For a review of the statistical methods used in near-real-time vaccine safety surveillance, see Leite et al. (2016).

title: Phase II multistage designs
text:
A single-arm phase II study asks whether a new treatment’s response rate \(p\) is promising enough for a randomised phase III trial:

\(H_0\!: p \le p_0\), an uninteresting rate;
\(H_1\!: p \ge p_1\), a promising rate.

The data are binary and the samples small, so everything is computed exactly from the binomial distribution, and the designs stop early mainly to avoid giving an ineffective treatment to more patients.

title: Phase II multistage designs
text:
A single-arm phase II study asks whether a new treatment’s response rate \(p\) is promising enough for a randomised phase III trial:

\(H_0\!: p \le p_0\), an uninteresting rate;
\(H_1\!: p \ge p_1\), a promising rate.

The data are binary and the samples small, so everything is computed exactly from the binomial distribution, and the designs stop early mainly to avoid giving an ineffective treatment to more patients.

title: Phase II multistage designs
text:
Frequentist multistage designs
Gehan (1961). The earliest two-stage plan: stop after the first stage if no responses are seen; otherwise enrol enough patients to estimate \(p\) with a given precision (Gehan 1961).
Simon’s two-stage design. Enrol \(n_1\) patients and stop for futility if there are \(r_1\) or fewer responses. Otherwise enrol up to \(n\) in total, and declare the treatment promising if there are more than \(r\) responses. Writing \(X_1 \sim \mathrm{Bin}(n_1, p)\) and \(X_2 \sim \mathrm{Bin}(n - n_1, p)\),
\[
P(\text{declare promising} \mid p) = \sum_{x_1 = r_1 + 1}^{n_1} P(X_1 = x_1)\; P(X_2 > r - x_1),
\]
\[
\mathrm{PET}(p) = P(X_1 \le r_1), \qquad E_p[N] = n_1 + \{1 - \mathrm{PET}(p)\}(n - n_1).
\]
Among all designs with type I error \(\le \alpha\) at \(p_0\) and power \(\ge 1-\beta\) at \(p_1\):

the optimal design minimises \(E_{p_0}[N]\);
the minimax design minimises the maximum \(n\) (Simon 1989).

Admissible designs are the compromises between the two that minimise a weighted combination of \(E_{p_0}[N]\) and \(n\) (Jung et al. 2004). Fleming (1982) gave a multistage (more than two stages) procedure. Bryant and Day (1995) added toxicity as a second endpoint.
Inference after a two-stage design. The naive proportion and p-value ignore the early-stopping option. Koyama and Chen (2008) describe proper p-values and confidence intervals.

title: Phase II multistage designs
text:
Bayesian designs

Posterior monitoring (Thall and Simon 1994). Stop if the posterior probability that the new treatment beats the standard by a margin falls below a threshold.
Predictive probability (Lee and Liu 2008). At each interim look, compute the probability that the trial will end with a positive posterior conclusion if it continues to its maximum size. With a Beta prior this is a finite sum of beta-binomial probabilities. Stop for futility if it is below \(\theta_L\), and for efficacy if it is above \(\theta_U\).
BOP2 (Zhou et al. 2017). Calibrates posterior-probability boundaries so that the design has a specified type I error, and extends them to joint efficacy–toxicity endpoints.

As with any Bayesian rule, the frequentist operating characteristics of these designs are computed and reported (see Bayesian monitoring).

title: Sequential probability ratio tests
text:
Group sequential designs look a few times. The sequential probability ratio test (SPRT) of Wald (1945) looks after every observation. It compares two simple hypotheses, \(H_0\!: \theta = \theta_0\) and \(H_1\!: \theta = \theta_1\), through the cumulative log-likelihood ratio
\[
\Lambda_n = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \log \frac{f(x_i \mid \theta_1)}{f(x_i \mid \theta_0)} .
\]
Sampling continues while \(\log B < \Lambda_n < \log A\). The test accepts \(H_1\) when \(\Lambda_n \ge \log A\) and accepts \(H_0\) when \(\Lambda_n \le \log B\). Wald’s approximations
\[
A \approx \frac{1-\beta}{\alpha}, \qquad B \approx \frac{\beta}{1-\alpha}
\]
give error rates slightly below the targets, because they ignore the overshoot of the boundary. Among all tests with the same error rates, the SPRT has the smallest expected sample size at both \(\theta_0\) and \(\theta_1\). The expected sample size is approximately
\[
E_\theta[N] \approx \frac{L(\theta)\log B + \{1 - L(\theta)\}\log A}{E_\theta[z]},
\]
where \(L(\theta)\) is the probability of accepting \(H_0\) and \(z\) is the log-likelihood ratio of a single observation (Wald 1947).

title: Sequential probability ratio tests

Example: a binomial SPRT

title: Sequential probability ratio tests
text:
Truncation and closed tests
The SPRT has no maximum sample size: under intermediate values of \(\theta\) it can run for a long time. Truncated SPRTs stop at a maximum \(N\) and decide there. Armitage (1957) proposed restricted procedures with a guaranteed maximum. The triangular test is the best-known closed alternative: its lines converge, so it always ends.
Truncating the binomial SPRT above at \(N = 60\) changes little, because few paths are still open at 60 patients. If the test rejects \(H_0\) at \(N\) whenever \(\Lambda_N > 0\), the type I error becomes 0.046. If it rejects \(H_0\) only at the upper line, the type I error is 0.039, the power drops to 0.801, and the expected sample size under \(H_0\) is 16.3. The continuous triangular test for the same hypotheses always stops by \(n = 58\). Its boundaries are approximations for data observed one at a time: here the exact type I error is 0.061 and the power 0.873. The exact values should be checked before such a design is used.

title: Sequential probability ratio tests
text:
Unknown variance: the sequential t-test
For normal data with unknown variance, the likelihood ratio of the \(t\) statistic under \(\delta = \delta_1\) against \(\delta = 0\) (a ratio of noncentral and central \(t\) densities) plays the role of \(\Lambda_n\). This gives the one-sample sequential t-test of Rushton (1950) and the two-sample test of Hajnal (1961). Psychology has rediscovered the approach as the “SPRT t-test” (Schnuerch and Erdfelder 2020), extended it to ANOVA (Steinhilber et al. 2024), and compared it with sequential Bayes factors (Stefan et al. 2022). Lakens (2014) discusses sequential analysis for experimental research more generally.

title: Bayesian sequential monitoring
text:
A Bayesian analysis combines a prior for the effect \(\theta\) with the data. With the normal approximation used throughout this tutorial — an estimate \(\hat\theta_k\) with information \(I_k\) — and a normal prior \(\theta \sim N(\mu_0, 1/I_0)\), the posterior at look \(k\) is
\[
\theta \mid \text{data} \sim N\!\left(\frac{I_0\mu_0 + I_k\hat\theta_k}{I_0 + I_k},\; \frac{1}{I_0 + I_k}\right).
\]
The prior can be expressed as “worth \(I_0\) units of information”.

A sceptical prior centred on no effect tempers early enthusiasm.
An enthusiastic prior centred on \(\theta_1\) tempers early pessimism.

Reporting the conclusions under both is informative (Spiegelhalter et al. 1994).
Typical monitoring rules are:

Efficacy: stop if \(P(\theta > \delta \mid \text{data}) \ge \gamma_E\), for a clinically relevant \(\delta\) (often 0).
Futility: stop if the predictive probability of a successful final analysis is below \(\gamma_F\). The predictive probability averages over the data still to come, given the current posterior.

Berry (2006) reviews Bayesian clinical trials; the same ideas underlie the phase II designs of Thall and Simon (1994) and Lee and Liu (2008).

section: The likelihood principle does not remove the frequentist error
text:
The likelihood principle does not remove the frequentist error
The posterior does not depend on the stopping rule, so a Bayesian analysis needs no multiplicity adjustment in its own terms. But the frequentist probability that a Bayesian rule declares efficacy when the treatment does not work still grows with the number of looks. With a flat prior, “stop if \(P(\theta > 0 \mid \text{data}) \ge 0.975\)” is the same as “stop if \(Z_k \ge 1.96\)”. Its type I error is that of repeated significance testing:

title: Bayesian sequential monitoring
text:
Sequential Bayes factors
In experimental psychology, a popular alternative is the sequential Bayes factor (SBF) design. Data are added until the Bayes factor \(\mathrm{BF}_{10}\) exceeds an evidence threshold \(k\) (for \(H_1\)) or falls below \(1/k\) (for \(H_0\)) (Schönbrodt et al. 2017). For \(t\)-tests the usual choice is the default JZS prior, a Cauchy distribution on the standardised effect size (Rouder et al. 2009).
Planning uses Bayes factor design analysis: simulation of the distribution of the stopping sample size and of the rates of misleading evidence (Schönbrodt and Wagenmakers 2018). Rouder (2014) discusses how to interpret optional stopping from a Bayesian viewpoint. Stefan et al. (2022) compare the efficiency of SBF designs with the SPRT.

title: Bayesian sequential monitoring
section: Example: a sequential Bayes factor design
text:
Example: a sequential Bayes factor design
A two-sample sequential Bayes factor design tests after every patient from 10 per group, stops when \(\mathrm{BF}_{10} \ge 10\) or \(\le 1/10\), and caps the study at 100 per group (default JZS prior, \(r = 0.707\)). Bayes factor design analysis by simulation (1000 runs) gives:

Effect \(d = 0.5\): evidence for \(H_1\) in 82 % of the studies, with 114 patients on average.
No effect: misleading evidence for \(H_1\) in 3.3 %, and never evidence for \(H_0\). With at most 100 per group, \(\mathrm{BF}_{01}\) cannot exceed 6.5, even if the two groups have identical means.

Evidence for \(H_0\) accumulates slowly, roughly like \(\sqrt{n}\), so the maximum sample size must be chosen with it in mind. The rate of misleading evidence has a simple bound: the JZS Bayes factor for the \(t\)-test is itself an e-process (it equals the “eCauchy” e-value of Grünwald et al. (2024)). By Ville’s inequality (see anytime-valid inference), the probability that it ever reaches \(k\) under \(H_0\) is at most \(1/k\), here 0.1. On the example data (Sequential outcomes), the Bayes factor reaches 10 after 72 patients.

title: Phase II with a predictive biomarker
text:
Many phase II trials now enrol patients with and without a biomarker that may predict benefit (BM+ and BM−), and they have two aims:

Go / no-go. Is the new treatment worth a phase III trial?
Which population. Does the biomarker select the patients who benefit, so that phase III should enrol BM+ patients only?

The answer is one of four recommendations for phase III (Freidlin et al. 2012):







Recommendation
When




Stop (no further testing)
no convincing benefit


BM+ only (enrichment design)
benefit in BM+, benefit in BM− ruled out


Biomarker-stratified design
benefit in BM+, BM− uncertain


All-comers (standard design)
benefit in both, or overall



So a design is judged by the probability of each recommendation under a few true-effect scenarios, not by one type I error and one power.
Three facts shape these designs (McShane et al. 2009; Polley et al. 2013; Freidlin and Korn 2013; Renfro et al. 2016):

A single-arm trial cannot show that a biomarker is predictive. A higher response rate in BM+ may mean the biomarker is prognostic (BM+ patients do better on any treatment). Single-arm results speak to predictiveness only if credible historical rates exist for each stratum. Randomized trials answer the question directly.
Phase II trials cannot be powered for an interaction test. A trial with 80 % power for the overall effect has only about 29 % power to detect an interaction of the same size; detecting it needs about four times the patients (Brookes et al. 2004). The designs therefore apply a sequence of decisions to the effect in each stratum. The interaction, and Gail and Simon’s test for a qualitative interaction (effects in opposite directions) (Gail and Simon 1985), are reported but do not drive the decision.
The BM+ estimate that triggers enrichment is optimistic (it was selected for being large), so phase III should not be sized from it naively.

title: Phase II with a predictive biomarker
section: Randomized designs: the algorithm of Freidlin et al.
text:
Randomized designs: the algorithm of Freidlin et al.
Patients are randomized within each stratum. On the benefit scale \(\theta\) (\(-\log\) HR, with HR experimental : control, or the difference in response rates), stratum \(s\) gives \(Z_s \approx N(\theta_s \sqrt{I_s}, 1)\), where \(I_s\) is the information (\(d_s/4\) for \(d_s\) events with 1:1 allocation (SCHOENFELD 1981)). The decision algorithm (Freidlin et al. 2012):

BM+ test. If \(Z_+ > z_{1-\alpha_1}\) (one-sided \(\alpha_1 = 0.10\)), go to step 3.
Otherwise, overall test. If the stratified \(Z = (\sqrt{I_+} Z_+ + \sqrt{I_-} Z_-)/\sqrt{I_+ + I_-}\) exceeds \(z_{1-\alpha_2}\) (\(\alpha_2 = 0.05\)), recommend all-comers; otherwise stop.
BM− effect. From the two-sided 80 % confidence interval of the HR in BM−: entirely above 0.77 (1/1.3) → BM+ only; entirely below 0.67 (1/1.5) → all-comers; otherwise → biomarker-stratified phase III.

The BM+ stratum is sized for the power target (90 % at HR 0.5), and the BM− stratum by the prevalence (natural accrual) or by a fixed ratio.
Exact operating characteristics. The strata are independent, so most recommendation probabilities are products of normal probabilities. Only the overall test couples the strata; it needs one integral over \(Z_+\), computed by Gauss–Legendre quadrature. With an interim futility look the within-stratum statistics are bivariate normal, handled with Genz’s algorithm (Genz 2004). With accrual at the natural prevalence, the probabilities are averaged exactly over the binomial number of BM+ patients.

title: Phase II with a predictive biomarker
text:
Single-arm designs
Without a control arm, each stratum is compared with an uninteresting response rate. The designs enrol a first stage in both strata and then choose a route:

Parallel designs: an independent Simon two-stage design in each stratum (each at \(\alpha/2\)).
Adaptive parallel designs (Jones and Holmgren 2007): if BM− shows enough responses at stage 1, both strata continue (unselected route); otherwise, if BM+ does, only BM+ continues (enrichment); otherwise the trial stops. At the end, enough BM− responses mean all-comers, and otherwise enough BM+ responses mean BM+ only.
Optimal stratified two-stage designs (Parashar et al. 2016): the same routes, with early stopping when a final cut-off is already reached, and the ten sample sizes and cut-offs chosen to minimise the expected sample size under \(H_0\) subject to

\(P(\text{any go} \mid p_0^-, p_0^+) \le \alpha\);
\(P(\text{all-comers} \mid p_1^-) \ge 1 - \beta\);
\(P(\text{BM+ only} \mid p_0^-, p_1^+) \ge 1 - \beta\).

Isotonic rules (Li and Ivanova 2024): the same routes, but each stratum is judged against the pooled rate when the observed rates contradict the expected order (\(p^- \le p^+\)).

With the stage-1 counts of the two strata independent, the three routes to a positive result factor into BM− and BM+ parts: \(P(\text{all-comers}) = S\), \(P(\text{BM+ only}) = (C - S)\,T + (1 - C)\,E\), where \(C\) is the probability that BM− continues, \(S\) that it succeeds, \(T\) that BM+ succeeds on the unselected route and \(E\) on the enrichment route. The module enumerates the three parts separately, keeps only the undominated ones, and combines them by branch and bound on the expected size. It finds all eight optimal designs of Table IV of Parashar et al. (2016), in seconds for most of them.
Li & Ivanova’s published designs. Under the rules as stated in their paper, the designs in the tables of Li and Ivanova (2024) have a type I error slightly above 0.05 (0.054 to 0.060); the module evaluates user-defined designs with these rules, exactly, rather than searching.
Time to event. Single-arm designs use the rate of patients alive and event-free at a landmark (for example 6 months), converted from medians under exponential survival. All patients must be followed to the landmark.
Natural prevalence. The published single-arm designs fix the number of patients per stratum (enrolment continues until each stratum is full). If all-comers are enrolled instead, the stratum sizes vary; the module then re-derives each cut-off at the realised size, keeping its planned null tail probability, and averages the operating characteristics exactly over the sizes. title: Information and the canonical joint distribution
text:
The canonical joint distribution
Let \(\hat\theta_k\) be the estimate at look \(k\) and \(Z_k = \hat\theta_k \sqrt{I_k}\) the standardised statistic. For a very wide class of models,
\[
Z_k \sim N\!\left(\theta\sqrt{I_k},\, 1\right), \qquad
\operatorname{Cov}(Z_j, Z_k) = \sqrt{I_j / I_k} \quad (j \le k).
\]
Equivalently, the score statistics \(S_k = Z_k\sqrt{I_k}\) have independent increments: \(S_k - S_{k-1} \sim N\!\left(\theta (I_k - I_{k-1}),\; I_k - I_{k-1}\right)\). This holds exactly for normal data with known variance, and asymptotically for maximum-likelihood estimates in regular parametric models, generalised linear models, the log-rank test and Cox regression (Tsiatis 1982; Jennison and Turnbull 1997; Scharfstein et al. 1997).
The consequence is powerful: boundaries, power and expected sample size depend only on the information fractions, not on the endpoint. A design is solved once on the \(Z\) scale, and the endpoint enters only when information is converted into patients or events (Sample size).

title: Information and the canonical joint distribution
text:
Brownian motion and the B-value
Lan and Wittes (1988) rescaled the statistic as the B-value \(B(t) = Z(t)\sqrt{t}\). Under the canonical distribution, \(B(t)\) is a Brownian motion with drift \(\eta = \theta\sqrt{I_{\max}}\):
\[
B(t) \sim N(\eta\, t,\; t), \qquad \text{independent increments}.
\]
Under \(H_0\) the drift is zero; under the design alternative it is \(\eta_1 = \theta_1\sqrt{I_{\max}}\). This picture makes several later results almost immediate, such as conditional power (Monitoring).

section: Fixed-sample information and the inflation factor
text:
Fixed-sample information and the inflation factor
A fixed-sample, one-look study with one-sided level \(\alpha\) and power \(1-\beta\) at \(\theta_1\) needs
\[
I_{\text{fix}} = \left(\frac{z_{1-\alpha} + z_{1-\beta}}{\theta_1}\right)^2 ,
\]
that is, a drift \(\eta_{\text{fix}} = z_{1-\alpha} + z_{1-\beta}\) (use \(\alpha/2\) for a two-sided test). A sequential design with stricter boundaries needs a larger drift \(\eta\) for the same power, so its maximum information is \(I_{\max} = R \cdot I_{\text{fix}}\), where \(R = (\eta/\eta_{\text{fix}})^2\) is the inflation factor.

title: Information and the canonical joint distribution
text:
How jmsequential computes
Probabilities of crossing the boundaries are obtained by recursive numerical integration of the density of \(Z_k\) over the region where the study continues (Armitage et al. 1969; Jennison and Turnbull 2000, ch. 19). The density at look \(k\) is evaluated on a grid of points; Simpson’s rule integrates it forward to look \(k+1\). This needs only the normal density and distribution functions, is exact to about \(10^{-8}\), and takes about a millisecond per design. It is the same algorithm used by gsDesign and rpact, and jmsequential’s implementation agrees with both to within \(10^{-5}\).

title: Beyond this module
text:
Group sequential designs allow only one kind of change: stopping. Adaptive designs also allow data-driven changes to the sample size, the arms or the population, while still controlling the type I error.

Combination tests. The stage-wise p-values are combined with a pre-specified function — Fisher’s product (Bauer and Kohne 1994) or the weighted inverse normal (Lehmacher and Wassmer 1999; Cui et al. 1999). The second stage can then be redesigned freely.
Conditional error function. Any modification is allowed if the conditional type I error of the original design is preserved (Proschan and Hunsberger 1995; Müller and Schäfer 2001).
Sample-size re-estimation. Unblinded re-estimation, for example the “promising zone” (Mehta and Pocock 2011), and blinded re-estimation or internal pilots (Friede and Kieser 2006). Jennison and Turnbull (2006) show that a well-chosen non-adaptive group sequential design is often as efficient.
Multi-arm multi-stage (MAMS), seamless phase II/III and enrichment designs (Magirr et al. 2012).

Reviews and practical guides: Bretz et al. (2009), Pallmann et al. (2018), Burnett et al. (2020) and Wassmer and Brannath (2016). Estimation after adaptive designs is reviewed by Robertson et al. (2023a) and Robertson et al. (2023b).

title: Beyond this module
text:
Trial sequential analysis (sequential meta-analysis)
A cumulative meta-analysis repeats its test whenever a new trial is added, with the same type I error inflation as a monitored trial. Trial sequential analysis applies Lan–DeMets boundaries to the cumulative \(Z\). It uses a required information size adjusted for heterogeneity (Wetterslev et al. 2008, 2017). For statistical methods for updating meta-analyses in living reviews see Simmonds et al. (2017). For an e-value alternative see ALL-IN meta-analysis (Schure and Grünwald 2022).

title: Beyond this module
text:
CUSUM and quality-control charts
The cumulative sum (CUSUM) chart (Page 1954) and its risk-adjusted version for surgical outcomes (Steiner 2000) monitor a process for a change, restarting after each signal. Their error control is expressed as the average run length before a false alarm, not as the type I and II errors of a single test. Reviews: Grigg and Farewell (2004) and Woodall (2006).

title: Interim monitoring
text:
The unblinded results go to the data monitoring committee (DMC). The statistician computes the current estimate, its standard error and \(Z_k\). The information fraction is \(t_k = I_k / I_{\max}\): events over planned events for survival, patients over planned patients otherwise. The boundaries are then recomputed at the observed \(t_k\) with the pre-specified spending function, and the result is compared with them (Lan and DeMets 1983; 2006). The boundaries guide the DMC; they do not replace its judgement, which also weighs safety, secondary outcomes and external evidence (DeMets and Ellenberg 2016).
Three practical points:

Unplanned timing. The number and timing of looks can differ from the plan, as long as the changes do not depend on the results (Lan and DeMets 1989).
Final look. At the final analysis all remaining \(\alpha\) is spent at the information actually obtained. This handles over- and under-running.
Non-binding futility. A non-binding futility boundary may be overruled without affecting \(\alpha\) (Futility).

title: Interim monitoring
text:
Conditional power
Conditional power is the probability of rejecting \(H_0\) at the end, given the data so far and an assumption about the true effect (Gordon Lan et al. 1982). With the B-value \(B = Z_k\sqrt{t_k}\) (Lan and Wittes 1988) and only the final analysis remaining,
\[
\mathrm{CP}(\eta) = 1 - \Phi\!\left(\frac{b_K - B - \eta\,(1 - t_k)}{\sqrt{1 - t_k}}\right),
\]
where \(\eta = \theta\sqrt{I_{\max}}\) is the drift assumed for the rest of the trial. Common choices are:

the design alternative, \(\eta_1\);
the current trend, \(\hat\eta = Z_k/\sqrt{t_k}\);
\(H_0\) (\(\eta = 0\)).

Very low conditional power under optimistic assumptions supports stopping for futility (stochastic curtailment) (Lachin 2005).

title: Interim monitoring
text:
Predictive power
Conditional power under the current trend treats a noisy estimate as the truth. Predictive power instead averages the conditional power over the uncertainty in the estimate. With a flat prior it is
\[
\mathrm{PP} = 1 - \Phi\!\left(\frac{b_K\sqrt{t_k} - Z_k}{\sqrt{1 - t_k}}\right)
\]
(Spiegelhalter et al. 1986).

title: Error-spending functions
text:
The alpha-spending function
An alpha-spending function \(\alpha(t)\) is non-decreasing on \([0, 1]\), with \(\alpha(0) = 0\) and \(\alpha(1) = \alpha\). It gives the cumulative type I error that may have been spent by information fraction \(t\). At each actual look \(k\), the boundary \(b_k\) is solved so that the probability of crossing it for the first time at that look is exactly the increment
\[
P_{H_0}\!\left(Z_1 < b_1, \dots, Z_{k-1} < b_{k-1},\ Z_k \ge b_k\right) = \alpha(t_k) - \alpha(t_{k-1}).
\]
The boundary at a look depends only on the looks already done, so the number and timing of future looks may change freely (provided the changes do not depend on the observed results) (Lan and DeMets 1989; DeMets and Lan 1994). At the final analysis all the remaining \(\alpha\) is spent, even if the information turns out larger or smaller than planned.
jmsequential applies the spending function to the level of one tail: \(\alpha\) for a one-sided design, and \(\alpha/2\) in each tail of a symmetric two-sided design. This is the gsDesign and rpact convention, and it reproduces the published Lan–DeMets tables.

title: Whitehead’s triangular tests
text:
Whitehead (1997) describes a sequential trial by two statistics:

the efficient score \(Z\), the numerator of the score test (for a difference in means it is proportional to the difference in sums);
its Fisher information \(V\), the null variance of \(Z\).

In the notation of this tutorial, \(V = I\) and \(Z = \hat\theta\, I\), the score statistic \(S\) of Information. The standardised statistic is \(Z/\sqrt V\). Under the canonical distribution, \(Z\) is a Brownian motion in “time” \(V\) with drift \(\theta\). Straight lines on this plane are therefore natural boundaries (Whitehead and Jones 1979; Whitehead 1999).

text:

the efficient score \(Z\), the numerator of the score test (for a difference in means it is proportional to the difference in sums);
its Fisher information \(V\), the null variance of \(Z\).

In the notation of this tutorial, \(V = I\) and \(Z = \hat\theta\, I\), the score statistic \(S\) of Information. The standardised statistic is \(Z/\sqrt V\). title: Whitehead’s triangular tests
text:
The triangular test
For a one-sided test of \(H_0\!: \theta \le 0\) against \(\theta = \theta_1 > 0\), with type I error \(\alpha\) and power \(1-\beta\), the triangular test continues while
\[
-a + 3cV \;<\; Z \;<\; a + cV ,
\]
rejecting \(H_0\) above the upper line and accepting it below the lower one. With \(k = 1 + z_{1-\beta}/z_{1-\alpha}\),
\[
a = \frac{k \,\ln\!\big(1/(2\alpha)\big)}{\theta_1}, \qquad c = \frac{\theta_1}{2k}.
\]
When \(\alpha = \beta\) these reduce to \(a = 2\ln(1/(2\alpha))/\theta_1\) and \(c = \theta_1/4\). The two lines meet at \(V_{\max} = a/c\), so the test is closed: it can never run beyond \(V_{\max}\). Among tests with the same error rates, it nearly minimises the maximum expected sample size (Whitehead and Stratton 1983; Jennison and Turnbull 2000).
Discrete looks. The formulas assume continuous monitoring. When the data are examined only at looks \(V_1 < V_2 < \dots\), a path can jump over a boundary between looks. The “Christmas-tree” correction pulls both boundaries in by \(0.583\sqrt{V_k - V_{k-1}}\) at look \(k\) (Whitehead 1997). The corrected boundaries therefore meet before the apex of the original triangle. jmsequential chooses the maximum information so that they meet exactly at the last planned look, as SAS PROC SEQDESIGN does, so every planned look can be reached. At that look, \(H_0\) is rejected if \(Z \ge 2cV\).
Two-sided alternative. The double triangular test joins two triangles, one for each sign of \(\theta\), each at level \(\alpha/2\). The region where both close becomes an inner wedge in which the trial stops with “no difference”.
jmsequential computes the boundaries from these formulas, then reports the exact attained \(\alpha\) and power from its numerical engine, because the formulas are approximations.

title: Classical group sequential boundaries
text:
A group sequential design plans \(K\) analyses, usually after equal increments of information. At look \(k\) the study stops and rejects \(H_0\) if \(|Z_k| \ge b_k\) (two-sided) or \(Z_k \ge b_k\) (one-sided). Otherwise it continues, and at the last look \(H_0\) is accepted. The boundaries \(b_1, \dots, b_K\) are chosen so that
\[
P_{H_0}\!\left(\text{cross } b_k \text{ at some look}\right) = \alpha .
\]
The classical designs give the boundaries a simple shape and solve a single constant \(C\) for the \(\alpha\) level. They assume the number and timing of looks are fixed in advance; the error-spending approach removes that assumption.

title: Classical group sequential boundaries

The boundaries \(b_1, \dots, b_K\) are chosen so that
\[

\]

title: Classical group sequential boundaries
text:
The main families
Pocock (1977). The same nominal level at every look: \(b_k = C\). For \(K = 5\) and two-sided \(\alpha = 0.05\), \(C = 2.413\), a nominal p-value of 0.016 at each look (Pocock 1977).
O’Brien–Fleming (1979). Very strict early, close to the fixed-sample value at the end: \(b_k = C\sqrt{K/k}\). For \(K = 5\), \(C = 2.040\), so the first look needs \(|Z| \ge 4.56\) (O’Brien and Fleming 1979).
Wang–Tsiatis (1987). A one-parameter family that contains both:
\[
b_k = C\, t_k^{\,\Delta - 1/2}, \qquad \Delta = 0 \ \text{(O'Brien–Fleming)}, \quad
\Delta = 0.5 \ \text{(Pocock)} .
\]
Intermediate values of \(\Delta\) trade early stopping against the final critical value (Wang and Tsiatis 1987).
Haybittle–Peto. A large fixed value at every interim look — typically \(|Z| \ge 3\), \(p < 0.0027\) — and almost the unadjusted value at the end (Haybittle 1971; Peto et al. 1976). It is easy to explain and barely changes the final analysis.
Wider families exist, notably the unified family of Kittelson and Emerson (1999), evaluated by their operating characteristics in Emerson et al. (2007).

The trade-off is clear from the tables:

Pocock stops early most often when the treatment works, but its maximum sample size is 21 % above the fixed design and its final test is much stricter than 1.96 — a trial that “just misses” at the end can be frustrating.
O’Brien–Fleming costs only 2.6 % extra at most and keeps the final boundary near 1.96. It rarely stops at the first look, which is usually what a monitoring committee wants when data are immature. This is why it (or its spending-function analogue) is the most common choice in confirmatory trials.
Haybittle–Peto behaves like O’Brien–Fleming in practice, with a simpler rule.

The expected sample size under \(H_0\) is the maximum: without a futility boundary, a trial of an ineffective treatment always runs to the end.
